story_titles: Why a map instead of a list
Why an instruction set is worth keeping
A chip for hobbyists and spacecraft
The ELF on the kitchen table
Notation as a tool of thought
One language for the whole building
A lab bench in the browser
A model you can see all of
Experts that specialise on their own
story_texts: You are on a painted map of the Software Wrighter projects. Each building is a field, each wing a subject, and each exhibit is real work you can run in your browser. Hover a building to see what it holds and click to walk in.
A list of repositories tells you nothing about how the work fits together. The campus puts related things near each other, so a walk through it is also a tour of the ideas.
This museum keeps machines alive as emulators. Every open wing has at least one system you can run: the IBM 1130 minicomputer, the System/360 and 390 mainframes, and the RCA 1802 microprocessor.
None of these machines runs on real hardware. Each is a program that behaves like the original, written so that its console, cards, and lights can be watched in a browser.

This wing is built around one machine, the IBM 1130, and everything that was plugged into it: the 1442 card read punch, the 2310 disk, the 1132 printer. The emulator in the middle of the room runs them together.
The wing also holds an assembler and utilities written recently to program the 1130 again, so a visitor can write a program, punch it to virtual cards, and watch it run.

IBM announced the 1130 in 1965 as a computer small and cheap enough for a single engineering department or a college laboratory. It was a 16-bit machine, usually programmed in Fortran, and many people wrote their first program on one.
The 2310 disk cartridge sat inside the console desk. It held about half a million words and gave the 1130 a disk operating system when many small computers still lived on cards and tape.

Operators learned to read the console lights the way a driver reads a dashboard. A program in a tight loop made a pattern you could recognise across the room, and the emulator reproduces those patterns.
This wing treats an instruction set as a museum piece. The first installation is the RCA CDP1802, and its exhibit lets you assemble code for the chip and watch it step through the program.
Hardware wears out, but an instruction set can be preserved exactly. Once the emulator is right, every program ever written for the chip runs again.

The RCA CDP1802, introduced in 1976, was an 8-bit CMOS microprocessor. Its low power use made it a favourite for hobby computers like the COSMAC ELF and for spacecraft, including the Galileo probe to Jupiter.

The COSMAC ELF was described in Popular Electronics in 1976 as a computer you could build for about a hundred dollars, with toggle switches for input and a pair of hex displays for output. The emulator here reproduces that panel.
The 1802 has sixteen 16-bit registers, and any of them can serve as the program counter. Switching which register is the program counter is how the chip calls a subroutine without a stack.
The wings here are about making things run: a small CPU called COR24, languages implemented on it, an operating system, emulators, and the tools that tie them together.
Most exhibits in this building share a substrate, the COR24 processor. A language built on it can run in a browser because the processor itself is emulated there.
Every language here is a working implementation you can type into: Tiny C, Pascal, Forth, a Lisp, APL, BASIC, SNOBOL4 and others, each running on the emulated COR24.
Implementing a language is the surest way to understand it. Each interpreter in this wing is small enough to read, and the differences between them show what each language decided to make easy.

APL began as a mathematical notation invented by Kenneth Iverson in the late 1950s for describing algorithms. It became a programming language when IBM implemented it in the 1960s, and its one-symbol operators still look like nothing else.

Each APL glyph is a whole operation on an array: reverse, sort, sum along an axis. A program that would be a page in another language is often a single line, which is why APL keyboards and fonts became part of its culture.
APL was one of the first languages used at a terminal, typing an expression and seeing the answer at once. The exhibit keeps that feel: type a line, get an array back.

This institute holds the sw-ml-study family: an array language built for machine learning, and the mathematics, algorithms, and machine learning experiments written in it. Every exhibit here can run in your browser.
Every exhibit in this building is written in sw-MLPL, an array language made for machine learning. The same interpreter that runs on a laptop also runs in the browser, which is how the demos travel.

This wing keeps microscopes: programs that record every intermediate value of a training run so you can watch a model learn instead of reading about it. It also holds a lab bench that trains tiny networks in your browser.
The neural network lab bench trains small networks on AND, OR, XOR, and a quadrant task while you watch the weights move. It is the simplest honest picture of what training is.

The MoE Microscope is a mixture-of-experts language model of a few thousand parameters, built one mechanism at a time so that every router decision and every expert can be looked at. Larger models hide these parts; this one is small enough to show them.

The docent you are talking to was trained in the microscope on sentences generated from this campus catalog. It predicts only what you want and where to send you; every word it says comes from the catalog, which is why it cannot invent an exhibit.

Nobody assigns subjects to the experts. The model is trained, the routing is measured, and the experts turn out to have split the work between themselves; the microscope shows that map rather than assuming it.

status_texts: The campus is a painted mockup today: you can hover, click, and follow directories, and the interactive application that replaces it is planned.
Three wings are open with running emulators; the other wings and the lobby exhibits are placeholders that say opening soon.
The 1130 system emulator runs; the wing's other peripherals, the 1442 card reader and its radio demo among them, are still being added.
The emulator runs the 1130 system in the browser today; it is usable, and it keeps gaining peripherals and polish.
One installation so far, the RCA CDP1802; other instruction sets are planned.
Both demos run today: the COSMAC ELF assembly emulator and the input and output demo.
Several wings are open with live demos on the COR24 processor, and the building's hardware interfaces wing is still planned.
Most languages in this wing run in the browser today; a few, such as the Fortran compiler, are research-phase.
The APL interpreter runs on the emulated COR24 in the browser today and is usable; it is a small interpreter, not a full APL system.
Several wings are open: the sw-MLPL playground, the mathematics wings, and the machine learning wing with two browser demos; the MoE Microscope live demo for this lobby is planned.
Two demos run in the browser today, the serial-MoE FPGA emulator and the neural network lab bench; the two microscopes are in progress.
The repository is public with its diagrams and measured results, and the docent you are talking to was trained there; the live demo page that steps through the model is planned and not published yet.
